verses.text: Then the Pharisees and Sadducees came and tested Jesus by asking Him to show them a sign from heaven.
But He replied, "When evening comes, you say, 'The weather will be fair, for the sky is red,'
and in the morning, 'Today it will be stormy, for the sky is red and overcast.' You know how to interpret the appearance of the sky, but not the signs of the times.
A wicked and adulterous generation demands a sign, but none will be given it except the sign of Jonah." Then He left them and went away.
When they crossed to the other side, the disciples forgot to take bread.
"Watch out!" Jesus told them. "Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees."
They discussed this among themselves and concluded, "It is because we did not bring any bread."
Aware of their conversation, Jesus said, "You of little faith, why are you debating among yourselves about having no bread?
Do you still not understand? Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many basketfuls you gathered?
Or the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many basketfuls you gathered?
How do you not understand that I was not telling you about bread? But beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees."
Then they understood that He was not telling them to beware of the leaven used in bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.
When Jesus came to the region of Caesarea Philippi, He questioned His disciples: "Who do people say the Son of Man is?"
They replied, "Some say John the Baptist; others say Elijah; and still others, Jeremiah or one of the prophets."
"But what about you?" Jesus asked. "Who do you say I am?"
Simon Peter answered, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God."
Jesus replied, "Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah! For this was not revealed to you by flesh and blood, but by My Father in heaven.
And I tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build My church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.
I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven."
Then He admonished the disciples not to tell anyone that He was the Christ.

From that time on Jesus began to show His disciples that He must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things at the hands of the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and that He must be killed and on the third day be raised to life.
Peter took Him aside and began to rebuke Him. "Far be it from You, Lord!" he said. "This shall never happen to You!"
But Jesus turned and said to Peter, "Get behind Me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to Me. For you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men."
Then Jesus told His disciples, "If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me.
For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake will find it.
What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world, yet forfeits his soul? Or what can a man give in exchange for his soul?
For the Son of Man will come in His Father's glory with His angels, and then He will repay each one according to what he has done.
Truly I tell you, some who are standing here will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming in His kingdom."

context.author: Matthew, writing to a Jewish audience
context.genre: Narrative with central teaching — a confrontation over signs, a private confession of Jesus' identity, and the first prediction of His death.
context.audience: Jewish-Christian readers watching the story pivot: from public ministry and miracles toward Jerusalem, the cross, and what following Jesus will actually cost.
context.setting: Caesarea Philippi sat at the base of Mount Hermon, a region filled with pagan shrines, including a grotto dedicated to the god Pan — a strikingly public, idol-filled backdrop for Peter's confession of Jesus as "the Son of the living God." The Pharisees and Sadducees, normally opposed to each other, unite here in testing Jesus.
context.custom: "Leaven" as a teaching metaphor (v.6-12) drew on something every listener understood physically — a small amount of yeast permeates an entire batch of dough, exactly how Jesus describes false teaching spreading quietly through a community.
context.timelineImmediate: A hinge point in the Gospel — Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi is followed immediately by Jesus' first direct prediction of His coming death and resurrection in Jerusalem, a turn the narrative has been building toward since chapter 1.
context.timelineBible: "The Christ, the Son of the living God" (v.16) directly invokes the royal covenant God made with David in 2 Samuel 7:12-16 — Peter isn't just calling Jesus a good teacher, he's identifying Him with a centuries-old promise of a coming King.

translation.meaning: A miraculous proof demanded on request — Jesus again refuses this kind of sign, pointing back to "the sign of Jonah" from chapter 12.
"Anointed One" — the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew "Messiah," God's promised King.

occurrences.note: One of the most common words in the whole New Testament — hundreds of uses across the Gospels, Acts, and every epistle.

translation.meaning: A distinct word from "Peter" (Petros, meaning a small stone) — the foundation Jesus builds on is debated as either Peter himself or the truth Peter just confessed.
This is the very first use of the word in Matthew's Gospel — an assembly or gathering, here referring to the community Jesus will build.

occurrences.note: Matthew uses this word only twice in his whole Gospel (here and in 18:17) — it becomes far more central later, especially in Acts and Paul's letters.

translation.meaning: To disown or renounce — the same verb family used later for Peter's own denial of Jesus, giving this call to discipleship real weight in hindsight.

gospelParallels.note: Mark's parallel account of Peter's confession and the first passion prediction.
Luke's shorter version of the same confession and rebuke.
Mark's parallel to the call to deny oneself and take up the cross.

otBackground.note: The Davidic covenant behind the title "Christ" Peter uses in his confession.
Jonah's three days in the fish — the sign Jesus again points to instead of a new miracle.
"The stone the builders rejected" — later applied to Jesus as the rock/cornerstone, connected to the imagery in v.18.

context.sparkNotes: Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ, and Jesus immediately predicts His coming death for the first time, rebuking Peter when he objects. The wordplay on "rock" here is deliberate — a different Greek word from "Peter" himself — and closes with Jesus quoting Psalm 118:22's rejected cornerstone, a verse He'll return to again in chapter 21.

commentary.note: Henry is careful about what the "rock" actually is: "without doubt Christ himself is the Rock, the tried foundation of the church... Peter's confession is this rock as to doctrine" — the truth Peter spoke, not merely the man who spoke it, is what the church is built on.

On the keys, Bengel makes a precise textual observation: Jesus says "the keys of the kingdom of heaven," not "of the Church" and not "of the kingdoms of the world" — a deliberately narrower scope than later tradition sometimes assumed, tied specifically to admission into the kingdom itself.

Clarke reads the "leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees" as false doctrine working exactly like literal leaven — quietly permeating and reshaping an entire mindset from within. He breaks "deny himself" into a deliberate progression: renouncing self-dependence, accepting whatever hardship following Christ brings, and imitating Jesus' own example step by step.
